newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Bushmen seek sanctuary in nature reserve.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bushmen seek sanctuary in nature reserve.

text.p: They were among the earliest inhabitants of South Africa, but persecution over the centuries by white and black invaders has left them with no land and a bleak future.

Now the country's remaining bands of Bushmen are trying to persuade President Nelson Mandela's democratic government to give them rights to a stretch of the Kalahari desert where their ancestors lived as hunter-gatherers.
Part of the land they claim lies in the Kalahari Gemsbok Park, a nature reserve named for a graceful oryx antelope that is adapted to the region's extreme heat and aridity.

The Land Claims Commission set up by Mandela's government to redress South Africa's racially skewed land ownership legacy has formally recognised the Bushmen's case as valid and has told the community to negotiate a deal with the National Parks Board, which runs the nature reserve.
If negotiations fail, then the issue would go to a special land claims court.
Louis Liebenberg, who is mediating between the Bushmen and the park authorities, said it would be in the interests of both sides to strike a deal giving Bushmen access to the park.

But Liebenberg, who has close ties to the Bushmen after years of researching their animal tracking skills, said negotiations could be difficult because some wildlife managers would not brook having Bushmen roam the Gemsbok park.

"Some of the parks people have been fairly negative, they regard it as ecologically unsound. Current parks board people have the philosophy that a national park must be sacrosanct and pristine, that you must keep humans out," Liebenberg said.
He said he had proposed that the Bushmen be granted a combination of ownership rights outside the park and land use rights inside the park.
These rights could include a concession for a game lodge inside the reserve and permission to collect medicinal plants.
"The idea is to try to find a spectrum of economic opportunities that communities can have access to that are not threatening the conservation status of the land," Liebenberg said.
"By maximising economic benefits to communities you also enhance protection of your national parks because it becomes in the interests of the communities to protect those parks."

Many anthropologists and historians accept that Bushmen, who have left their distinctive rock paintings in caves across southern Africa, were living in the region before the darker- skinned tribes who now dominate moved down from the north.

The Bushmen, whose name for themselves translates as "the harmless people", were driven into the least hospitable areas by these black settlers and by the whites who began arriving from Europe in the 17th Century.

Now there are estimated to be only 200 to 250 Bushmen surviving in South Africa, mainly descended from groups who were kicked out of the Gemsbok park after it was proclaimed in the 1930s. Several thousand more live in Botswana and Namibia.
"They've been dispersed, there's no sense of community," Liebenberg said.
"If you can put up a luxury lodge in the Gemsbok park, and have the Bushmen go into say a 50 percent joint venture with a private entrepreneur, the profits they could generate would be tremendous.
"They could have proper development -- there's no real future for them otherwise."
Attorney Roger Chennells is acting for the Bushmen in their land claim.
"It would be an absolutely unique event -- the return of the land of this dispersed, dispossessed and highly disempowered group," he said.

Chennells noted that the isolation of the Bushmen from organised society and their culture, including the credo that humans belong to the land rather than vice versa, created difficulties in the restitution process.

"They have a tendency, almost anarchistic in effect, to not act in a 'Western' or 'civilised' manner regarding matters of import...They are notorious for their Zen-like attitude to development in the Western context," he said.
One early white administrator despaired of trying to persuade Bushmen they were not allowed to hunt in game reserves.
"They profess to be unable to understand by what right the government protects the game and invariably ask to be shown the government brand on the animals," he wrote.
Anthropologist Hennie Steyn said South Africa's remaining Bushmen were faced with "the very real possibility of cultural extinction".

"None of the adults have lived by hunting/gathering for the last two decades... Restoring their traditional land rights in some way or other may provide the security crucial to their cultural survival," he said.
